definition: The smallest possible unit (quantum) of energy in the electromagnetic field at a given frequency; an elementary particle with no mass, no charge and no internal parts, carrying energy hf and momentum h/λ.
The smallest indivisible amount of some quantity; for light of frequency f, one quantum of energy is hf.
The constant linking a photon's energy to its frequency, E = hf; h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s = 4.136 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV·s.
The energy an electron gains crossing a potential difference of 1 volt; 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Convenient for photon and atomic energies.
The ejection of electrons from a material when light shines on it. Electrons are emitted only if each photon's energy exceeds the work function, regardless of brightness.
An electron ejected from a material by absorbing a photon.
The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of a material; about 2–6 eV for metals. It depends on the material, its surface condition and the exposed crystal face.
The lowest light frequency that can eject electrons from a given material, f₀ = φ/h. The corresponding threshold wavelength is λ₀ = hc/φ.
The reverse voltage that just stops the fastest photoelectrons from reaching the collector; it measures their kinetic energy, KE_max = eVₛ.
The number of photons arriving (or emitted) per second; for a beam of power P, Ṅ = P/(hf).
The momentum carried by a photon, p = h/λ = E/c, which is why light exerts a (tiny) pressure on surfaces it hits.
The fact that light (and matter) shows wave behavior in how it travels and particle behavior in how it is absorbed or emitted.
The stripes of bright and dark produced when waves from two or more paths overlap; built up dot by dot even when photons arrive one at a time.
A light detector that uses the photoelectric effect at a low-work-function surface, then multiplies each freed electron into a measurable pulse, sensitive enough to count single photons.
